paragraphs.heading: Primes two apart
paragraphs.text: A twin prime is a prime number that sits 2 away from another prime, like either number in the pair (17, 19) or (41, 43). Put another way, its prime gap is two. The term is also used for the pair itself, which may be called a prime twin or prime pair. The pair (2, 3) is usually left out, so the list begins with (3, 5), (5, 7) and (11, 13).

paragraphs.heading: Patterns in the pairs
paragraphs.text: Because 2 is the only even prime, (2, 3) is the only pair of primes just one apart, so twin primes are as close together as any other two primes can be. Every twin pair after (3, 5) has the shape (6n − 1, 6n + 1) for some natural number n, so the number between them is a multiple of 6. That is why 5 is the only prime that belongs to two pairs. It also means the sum of any twin pair other than 3 and 5 divides evenly by 12.

paragraphs.heading: Do they ever run out
paragraphs.text: Twin primes get rarer as you look at larger ranges, in line with the general tendency of gaps between primes to widen as numbers grow. Whether they stop altogether is unknown. The twin prime conjecture says there are infinitely many primes p for which p + 2 is also prime, and for many years this has ranked among the great unsolved questions of number theory. In 1849 de Polignac proposed a broader version: for every natural number k, infinitely many primes p have p + 2k prime too. The twin prime conjecture is his case k = 1.

paragraphs.heading: Zhang's breakthrough
paragraphs.text: Yitang Zhang announced on 17 April 2013 that he could prove that some integer N below 70 million is the gap between infinitely many pairs of primes. His paper was accepted in early May 2013. Terence Tao then proposed a Polymath Project, a collaborative effort, to bring Zhang's bound down. One year after the announcement the bound had fallen to 246, and James Maynard and Tao found improved bounds independently with a different, simpler approach than Zhang's.

paragraphs.heading: What the bound of 246 means
paragraphs.text: In plain terms, there are infinitely many primes whose next prime is at most 246 larger. Lowering that number to 2 would prove the twin prime conjecture. If the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture and its generalized form are assumed, the bound drops to 12 and 6 respectively. For now, though, the conjecture remains unsolved.

paragraphs.heading: Earlier steps
paragraphs.text: In 1940 Paul Erdős showed that for some constant c < 1, infinitely many primes p have a next prime p′ with p′ − p < c ln p. This means infinitely many stretches of numbers hold two primes, as long as the stretches may grow slowly, at a logarithmic rate, as the primes get bigger. In 1986 Helmut Maier showed the constant could be below 0.25. In 2004 Daniel Goldston and Cem Yıldırım pushed it down to 0.085786... .

paragraphs.heading: A law for twin primes
paragraphs.text: A stronger form of the conjecture, the first Hardy–Littlewood conjecture, named after Hardy and John Littlewood, proposes a distribution law for twin primes, much as the prime number theorem does for all primes. Let π₂(x) count the primes p ≤ x for which p + 2 is prime as well. If you assume that 1/(ln t) describes the density of primes, an assumption the prime number theorem suggests, the conjecture can be justified, though not proven. That same assumption implies the twin prime conjecture.
